source.section: Number of Factors and Sum of all Factors

problem.text:
The following number is the product of the divisors of $n$.
$$2^6\cdot 3^3$$
What is $n$?

steps.title: Where to start: the product-of-divisors formula
steps.body:
Divisors come in pairs $d$ and $\tfrac{n}{d}$ that multiply to $n$, so the product of all divisors is $n^{d(n)/2}$, where $d(n)$ is the number of divisors. Setting this equal to the given number and squaring removes the awkward half:
$$n^{d(n)} = 2^{12}\cdot 3^6$$

your_turn.answer: Only $2$ and $3$. Any other prime in $n$ would also show up in $n^{d(n)}$, but the right side has only $2$s and $3$s.

steps.title: Write $n$ with unknown exponents
steps.body:
Let $n = 2^a\cdot 3^b$. Then $d(n) = (a+1)(b+1)$, and raising $n$ to that power multiplies each exponent by $(a+1)(b+1)$. Matching the exponents of $2$ and of $3$ gives two equations:
$$a(a+1)(b+1) = 12, \qquad b(a+1)(b+1) = 6$$

your_turn.prompt: Divide the first equation by the second. What do you learn about $a$ and $b$?

steps.title: Solve for $b$
steps.body: Substitute $a = 2b$ into the second equation to get $b(2b+1)(b+1) = 6$. The left side grows fast as $b$ grows, so try small positive integers.

your_turn.answer: $b = 1$, since $1\cdot 3\cdot 2 = 6$. Already $b = 2$ gives $2\cdot 5\cdot 3 = 30$, which is too big.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: With $b = 1$ we get $a = 2b = 2$, so $n = 2^2\cdot 3^1 = 12$. Check: $12$ has $6$ divisors, and their product is $1\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdot 12 = 1728 = 12^3 = 2^6\cdot 3^3$. The answer is **12**.
